Additionally, land-based activities will affect Arctic fisheries, with favorable conditions making activities possible that were previously restricted due to lower temperatures. For example, farming will become feasible in coastal areas, posing the threat of negative effects on fisheries by pesticides.

Shipping and maritime navigation. There is strong demand for Arctic resources, particularly hydrocarbon resources, among emerging economies, such as China. This prompts a search for shorter routes and more efficient means of transport. The melting Arctic creates such an opportunity, as the new sea routes along the Arctic coast have been operational during the past decade. The Northern Sea Route (NSR), for example, is open for navigation for at least 3 months during summer time (Yeong-Seok and Jung 2014). An increase in investment in ice-class ship-building, infrastructural developments to connect land-sea interfaces and offer port facilities are all expected to keep the routes in operation even beyond the summer months. The longer they are open, the more they will attract maritime traffic and, at the same time, the more trade and investment through and along these sea routes are expected to grow. While the Northwestern Passage along the Canadian Arctic coast is not yet fully operational, the NSR has seen a gradual increase in shipping; the volume of cargo ships has risen constantly in recent years. As sea ice disappears with climate change and access to the Arctic Ocean improves, it is expected that the sea routes will be increasingly used as an alternative to the traditional mid-latitude routes such as the Suez Canal (Pruyn 2016). The Arctic sea routes, compared to traditional ones, are shorter in distance, saving time and energy in shipping (Furuich and Otsuka 2013). For example, a journey through the NSR from Shanghai, China, to Rotter- dam, the Netherlands, saves 2 weeks of time and translates into a savings of 40% of the energy previously needed. However, the Arctic sea routes are not yet well developed and pose many operational challenges due to the harsh climate and the lack of infrastructure such as port facilities, emergency rescue centres, roads, and physical network communications. Studies suggest that ship performance in ice conditions will gradually improve: compared to other routes, shipping currently saves 5 to 16% of costs; this savings is projected to increase to 29% by 2030 and 37% by 2050 (Peters et al. 2015).

As regards the increase in new forms of economic activity, developments in the Arctic aggravate tensions among actors and various interest groups over the issue of how much the Arctic as a region and its population are benefiting. The Arctic opening up creates easy access to fishery resources, yet there remains an uncertainty concerning the region’s fish stocks. In anticipation of this dilemma, the countries and actors having a stake in the Arctic concluded a moratorium, which entered into force in June 2021, restricting unregulated high seas fishing in the central Arctic Ocean for the next 16 years (CAO Fisheries. 2021).
